lenses.lens: Codebase audit of the existing radius/gravity laws in Well Dipper (read-only, no web research this run). Every claim below is traceable to a source line I read or a script I executed.
lenses.law:
AS-IMPLEMENTED (the composed chain that actually reaches the screen):

  (1) g(R) — TWO CONTRADICTORY LAWS LIVE IN THE REPO
      (1a) body-condition-vector.js:37   g = g_c · (R/R_c)          i.e. M ∝ R^3, g ∝ R^1.0   (constant density)
      (1b) src/generation/PhysicsEngine.js:72  M = 0.9·R^3.7 (rocky) i.e. g = M/R^2 ∝ R^1.7    (comment cites "Chen & Kipping")
      Symbols: R = radiusEarth (Earth radii), R_c = the preset's canonical radius, g in Earth-g,
      g_c = M_c/R_c^2 evaluated from the preset's declared massEarth (planet-lod-lab-core.js:611).
      NOTHING in the repo reconciles these. The exponent a in g = R^a is UNDERIVED: the world-engine
      path assumes a = 1.0, the game's own physics module assumes a = 1.7.

  (2) reliefEnvelope (planet-lod-lab-core.js:1100-1105)
      E(R,g) = clamp( g^(-Q) , F , C ),  Q = Q_RELIEF = 0.58, F = RELIEF_FLOOR = 0.40, C = RELIEF_CEIL = 133
      R is an accepted-but-UNUSED argument. Q is a least-squares fit through 5 authored "target"
      relief/R values (Earth 0.003, Mercury 0.004, Mars 0.006, Moon 0.012, Mimas 0.050), forced through
      Earth = 1. I re-ran the calibration script: it prints Q = 0.5774 → baked 0.58; C = 0.40/0.003 = 133.
      The script reports band membership only — NO residual, NO r^2, NO uncertainty on Q.

  (3) The ONE application to screen (world-engine-lab.html:5908)
      uPerturb = state.perturb · E(R, g_stashed)
      where g_stashed = u.surfaceGravity = M_c/R_c^2 — the CANONICAL PRESET gravity, NOT the drawn radius.
      Consequence: in the live render the relief envelope is RADIUS-BLIND. Dragging the radius slider
      changes uPerturb by exactly zero, contradicting the design note at :5907 ("Radius flows through g").

  (4) Composition into pixels (fragment shader)
      analytic path  : reliefAmp = uPerturb · mix(0.7, 1.0, uLodRamp) ; shadeN = perturbAnalytic(N, grad, reliefAmp)
                       perturbAnalytic (planet-lod-height.glsl.js:1489): N' = normalize(N - gTan·strength·0.6),
                       then a HARD saturation: if dot(N',N) < 0.5 → N' = normalize(mix(N',N,0.5)).
      finite-diff path: shadeN = perturbFiniteDiff(N, vPos, uPerturb)  — NO lodRamp term, internal
                       scale = strength·0.025. Same uniform, two different effective gains.
      grad source    : hd = baked·uReliefBakeStrength + synth·(1 - uReliefBakeStrength)
                       uReliefBakeStrength = base · bakeReliefCrossover(sVis),  bakeReliefCrossover(s) = 1 - smoothstep(0, 1.0, |log2 s|)
                       synth = fbmd(pos · uDispDomainScale, ...),  uDispDomainScale = sVis = visScaleOf(R) = R^0.5
      So: AMPLITUDE is a function of g only; CHARACTER and FREQUENCY are functions of R only, and only
      through the DISPLAY scale sVis. That inversion is the defect.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE (what the code should express, exponents to be set by the literature lens):
      E(R) = clamp( [R^a]^(-Q) , F(a,Q,R_max) , C ) = clamp( R^(-aQ) , F , C )
      with a fixed to ONE mass-radius exponent used repo-wide, and F re-derived rather than inherited.
      Under the repo's own two candidates the composed exponent aQ is 0.58 (a=1.0) or 0.99 (a=1.7) —
      a factor-1.7 difference in how fast relief dies with size. At present the code ships aQ = 0
      on screen (radius-blind, see (3)) while the CPU bake path ships aQ = 0.58.
lenses.validityRange:
ANCHORED: g ∈ [0.0065, 1.0] Earth-g, R ∈ [0.0017, 1.0] R⊕. Every fit anchor for Q_RELIEF is at or below Earth gravity (Earth g=1.0, Mercury 0.377, Mars 0.379, Moon 0.165, Mimas 0.00648). Phobos and Vesta are ceiling references only, and are also sub-Earth. The reliefBudget RELIC fit is worse: exactly 2 anchors, Mercury and Moon, both g < 0.38. K_DT = 3.1 is an LS fit to Earth/Mercury/Moon — again all g ≤ 1.

EXTRAPOLATION: everything at g > 1 / R > 1. There is not one super-Earth anchor anywhere in the calibration.

DEAD ZONE (worse than extrapolation — the law stops responding entirely):
- RELIEF_FLOOR = 0.40 binds at g ≥ 4.85 (a = 1.0 ⇒ R ≥ 4.85; a = 1.7 ⇒ R ≥ 2.53). Above that, relief is constant in g.
- glacialFlowVigor and chaosRaftJitter use clamp01(surfaceGravity) — identical to Earth for EVERY g ≥ 1.
- scarpStrength: smallness = clamp01((1.3 − R)/1.0) = 0 for all R ≥ 1.3 — identically zero on every super-Earth.
- lidStrength gMod = clamp(0.90, 1.12, (ρg/4.95)^0.15) saturates at ρg = 10.54, i.e. g ≈ 1.92 at ρ = 5.5.
- contractionDrive uses clamp01(g/1.5) — saturates at g = 1.5.
- edificeMaxHeight = clamp(1/g, 0.2, 2.0) floors at g = 5.
- bakeReliefCrossover reaches 0 at |log2 √R| ≥ 1, i.e. R ≥ 4 — baked plate tectonics is fully gone.

So on the specific question "what happens to a super-Earth", the honest answer from the source is: between R = 1.3 and R ≈ 5, one law after another silently saturates, and above R ≈ 4 the body is generic fBm.

lenses.contested:
Three genuine disagreements, two of them internal to this repo:

1. THE MASS-RADIUS EXPONENT IS UNRESOLVED IN THE CODEBASE ITSELF. body-condition-vector.js assumes constant density (g ∝ R^1.0); PhysicsEngine.js assumes M ∝ R^3.7 (g ∝ R^1.7). Both ship. The task brief anticipates a ≈ 0.5–1.0; note that the repo's own game-side value (1.7) sits ABOVE that bracket, so the brief's range and the code's range do not overlap at the top. This must be settled by the literature lens before anything downstream is retuned, because Q_RELIEF acts on g and the composed exponent aQ ranges from 0.58 to 0.99 across the two candidates. I did not do web research this run and cannot adjudicate it.

2. THE GRAVITY EXPONENT IN THE RELIEF LAW IS INTERNALLY CONTESTED. 0.58 (fit, 5 sub-Earth anchors, no residual reported) versus 0.50 (legacy, no source at all) both ship in different code paths, with different ceilings (133 vs 2.5) and different floor-binding gravities (4.85 vs 6.25). Whichever the literature supports, the repo currently answers the same question two ways.

3. WHETHER A RELIEF/GRAVITY LAW IS EVEN THE RIGHT SHAPE FOR SUPER-EARTHS. The calibration models apparent relief/R as linear in a single g^-Q multiplier. That is a strength-cap intuition (taller mountains slump under higher gravity), and it is not obviously the dominant control at high mass — mantle convection vigour, lithospheric thickness, and tectonic regime (mobile vs. stagnant lid) are all mass-dependent and could push relief either way. The repo's own e1Regime module models regime separately and its gravity lever saturates at g ≈ 1.9, so the two mechanisms are not composed. I flag this as a question for the literature lens rather than an answer: it is entirely possible the defensible finding is a bracket, not a law.

FINALLY, AND PLAINLY: there is no observational constraint on super-Earth topography. No super-Earth's relief has been measured. Any exponent chosen for g > 1 is extrapolation from Solar System bodies spanning g ∈ [0.0006, 1.0] — a range that stops exactly where the question begins. The most defensible thing the code could do is make that honesty structural: state the anchored range, state the extrapolation, and stop pretending a two-significant-figure constant fit to five sub-Earth bodies carries information about a 3 R⊕ world. What it should NOT keep doing is let a display lever (bakeReliefCrossover) decide the answer instead.

lenses.lens: Tectonic REGIME vs planet size — does a super-Earth have plate tectonics, and does the plate PATTERN (count, size, boundary spacing) change with planet radius?
lenses.law:
TWO LAWS. One is well-constrained and directly usable; the other is genuinely contested and must be encoded as a bracket, not a formula.

═══ LAW A (well-constrained) — SURFACE GRAVITY vs RADIUS ═══
  g(R)/g_E = (R/R_E)^a ,  a = 1.70   [bracket a ∈ 1.70–1.85]

Derivation: at FIXED bulk composition (fixed core mass fraction), Zeng, Sasselov & Jacobsen 2016 give
  R/R_E = (1.07 − 0.21·CMF)·(M/M_E)^(1/3.7)   [CMF only sets the prefactor, not the exponent]
so M ∝ R^3.7 and g = GM/R² ∝ R^(3.7−2) = R^1.70.
Valencia et al. 2007's independent interior models give g ∝ M^0.50 with R ∝ M^0.27 ⇒ a = 1.85.

⚠ THE BRIEF'S PREMISE IS BACKWARDS. The brief states "uncompressed constant density gives g ∝ R exactly; realistic compression softens the exponent" to a ≈ 0.5–1.0. Compression does the OPPOSITE: it makes big planets denser, so R grows more slowly than M^(1/3), so g rises FASTER than linearly in R. a = 1 is the incompressible LOWER bound; the real exponent is ~1.7. Any downstream law of the form f(g) is therefore being fed a g that is too small by (R^1.7 / R^0.75) — a factor 2.0 at R = 2, 3.6 at R = 3.

═══ LAW B (well-constrained WITHIN the mobile-lid branch) — PLATE PATTERN vs RADIUS ═══
  Characteristic plate linear dimension:   L(R) = 0.29 · R        (i.e. L ∝ R^1.00)
  Angular plate size on the sphere:        θ_plate ≈ L/R ≈ 0.29 rad ≈ 17°   — INVARIANT in R
  Plate count:                             N(R) = N_E · R^(−0.07) ≈ N_E ≈ 7–15   — INVARIANT in R
  Boundary spacing:                        s(R) ∝ R (scales with the planet, not with plate number)

Anchors: Valencia et al. 2007 Table 1 + §3 — plate length L = 1800 km at 1 M_E, L ∝ M^0.28 (T-dependent viscosity) / M^0.29 (isoviscous); plate thickness δ = 43 km at 1 M_E, δ ∝ M^−0.45; normal stress σ = 10 MPa, σ ∝ M^1.00. Combining L ∝ M^0.28 with R ∝ M^0.27 (Zeng 2016) gives L/R ∝ M^0.01. Valencia et al. state this explicitly: "The relative size of the convection cells measured as the length of the plate with respect to its radius (L/R) increases slightly, from a 0.29 for a 1M⊕ planet to a 0.30 ratio for a 10M⊕ planet."

Consequence for the renderer, stated bluntly: N ∝ R^(−0.07) means the plate count falls 5% from R = 1 to R = 2, and 8% from R = 1 to R = 3. **A fixed-N spherical Voronoi whose cells scale with the body IS the physically correct construction.** The existing generator's radius-independent PLATE_COUNT is not a bug — it is what the literature predicts. What is wrong is throwing the pattern away at large R.

═══ LAW C (CONTESTED — no formula is defensible; here is the bracket) ═══
Regime P(mobile | R) is NOT a resolvable function of R. Three literature positions, all still live in 2024:
  (i)   INCREASING with size — Valencia/O'Connell/Sasselov 2007; van Heck & Tackley 2011 (title states "equally or more likely"); Tackley et al. 2013.
  (ii)  DECREASING with size — O'Neill & Lenardic 2007 (mobile→episodic→stagnant with rising radius; their weak-lithosphere case stagnates at a scale factor of only ≈1.10 R_E); Stamenković et al. 2012 (pressure-dependent viscosity ⇒ sluggish deep mantle).
  (iii) SIZE IS NEARLY IRRELEVANT — Korenaga 2010: "the planetary size plays a rather minor role and … the likelihood of plate tectonics is controlled largely by the presence of surface water."

Lichtenberg & Miguel 2024 (Treatise on Geochemistry, 3rd ed.) survey exactly this list and conclude the theoretical models are "not reaching convergence (Lenardic 2018)," and further: "In the Solar System, Earth is the only planet that undergoes mobile lid tectonics at present day, all other planetary bodies exhibit a form of geodynamics closer to a stagnant lid. Therefore, stagnant lid geodynamics may be a better approximation for exoplanets."

DEFENSIBLE ENGINEERING FORM (encodes the disagreement instead of picking a winner):
  P_mobile = f(water/volatile fraction, surface temperature) · [1 + ε·ln R],  ε drawn per-body from a seeded distribution spanning [−0.3, +0.3]
i.e. water and surface T are the deterministic levers (Korenaga — the only position with a mechanism all three camps accept); radius enters only as a SEEDED sign-ambiguous nudge, because the sign of ∂P/∂R is the thing the field cannot agree on. Making regime a hard deterministic function of R would be asserting a resolution that does not exist.

═══ LAW D (the mobile branch's own upper bound — where even the pro-mobile camp stops giving you many plates) ═══
Even where 3D models keep the lid mobile, the PLANFORM lengthens at high mass. Tackley et al. 2013: "Convection in large super-Earths is characterised by large upwellings (even with zero basal heating) and small, time-dependent downwellings, which for large super-Earths merge into broad downwellings." Meier et al. 2021/2024 recover degree-1 HEMISPHERIC convection for a 1.34 R_E super-Earth under a strong lithosphere. So:
  R ≲ 1.5 R_E  →  N ≈ N_E ≈ 7–15, Law B holds
  R ≳ 1.5–2 R_E →  N collapses toward degree-1/degree-2 (1–2 hemispheric domains), NOT toward many small plates
Nothing in the retrieved literature — on either side of the controversy — predicts MORE, SMALLER plates on a larger planet. That direction is unsupported.

═══ WHAT SURFACE CHARACTER EACH REGIME MUST EXPRESS (the renderer's actual contract) ═══
  MOBILE LID  — global connected network of narrow linear belts; ~7–15 plates covering the sphere; boundary-localised relief (convergent ranges, divergent rifts, transform offsets); low-relief cratonic interiors; crater record erased and reset (young surface, fractal-tail small plates per Mallard et al. 2016, whose plate layout is set by SLAB SPACING — a lithosphere-thickness scale, not a planet-radius scale).
  STAGNANT LID — NO global boundary network. Surface = ancient impact-crater size-frequency distribution + discrete volcanic constructs (shields, calderas, coronae, tessera) + long-wavelength dynamic topography + a few big rift/graben systems. Structurally SPARSE and POINT/PATCH-dominated, not linear-network dominated. (Measured: Mercury, Mars, Moon, Venus.)
  EPISODIC — stagnant-lid character overprinted by globally-synchronous resurfacing events; patchwork of very-young and very-old terrain with sharp age boundaries. Venus's near-uniform crater age is the type case.

═══ THE fBm QUESTION (answered directly) ═══
Generic fBm as the SOLE low/mid-frequency source is wrong at EVERY radius, in BOTH regimes:
  • Mobile-lid: wrong because Law B says the pattern is a ~constant-count Voronoi network whose cells scale with R. fBm has no boundary network, no plate interiors, no convergent/divergent asymmetry.
  • Stagnant-lid: also wrong, because stagnant surfaces are not self-affine noise either — they are crater-SFD + discrete volcanic constructs + degree-1/2 dynamic topography. Substituting fBm here trades one wrong texture for another.
fBm is defensible ONLY as the sub-plate ROUGHNESS layer riding on top of a structured low-order field — never as the replacement for it.

═══ SECONDARY: audit of the existing Q_RELIEF envelope ═══
The standard isostatic/crustal-strength limit (textbook, Turcotte & Schubert-type) gives h_max ≈ σ_y/(ρ g), i.e. relief ∝ g^−1.0, Q = 1. The code's Q_RELIEF = 0.58 is a least-squares fit through Earth/Mercury/Mars/Moon/Mimas — every anchor at g ≤ 1 g_E, where SMALL-body strength (not isostasy) dominates and Q < 1 is expected. Extrapolating Q = 0.58 upward into g > 1 is fitting the wrong physical branch: for super-Earths the strength-limit branch (Q = 1) is the one that binds. With the corrected a = 1.7, at R = 2 the code multiplier is g^−0.58 = 0.505 while the strength limit gives g^−1 = 0.308 — a 1.6× relief overshoot, and absolute relief goes 20 km → 20.2 km (code, essentially flat) vs 20 km → 12.3 km (strength limit). Also: RELIEF_FLOOR = 0.40 binds at g ≥ 4.85, which under a = 1.7 is R = 2.53 R_E (a reachable super-Earth), not the ~R = 8 the a ≈ 0.75 premise would imply. The floor is a real, reachable, and physically unmotivated clamp.
lenses.validityRange:
LAW A (g ∝ R^1.70): calibrated over M = 1–8 M_E, CMF 0.0–0.4 (Zeng et al. 2016 PREM fit) ⇒ R ≈ 0.87–1.75 R_E for Earth-like composition. Extrapolation beyond R ≈ 1.8 R_E; the exponent is robust to CMF (CMF moves only the prefactor). Breaks entirely for volatile-rich / water-world / carbon compositions where the M-R relation is different.

LAW B (L/R ≈ 0.29, N ∝ R^−0.07): derived from Valencia et al. 2007's parameterized boundary-layer convection over M = 1–10 M_E ⇒ R ≈ 1–1.85 R_E. Conditional on being in the mobile-lid branch at all. It is a MODEL result from a 1D parameterized convection scaling, cross-checked against no observation of any exoplanet plate layout — because none exists.

LAW C (regime probability): contested over the ENTIRE range R > 1 R_E. There is no defensible formula; only the bracket. Below R = 1 R_E the picture is observationally grounded and one-sided — Mercury, Mars, the Moon and Venus are all measured to be stagnant-lid (Venus possibly episodic), so "small ⇒ not mobile" is the only size-regime statement with data behind it.

LAW D (planform collapse toward degree-1/2 above ~1.5–2 R_E): modelled only, from 3D compressible spherical/regional convection (Tackley et al. 2013; Meier et al. 2021, 2024). Sensitive to the assumed lithospheric yield stress; not a hard threshold.

HARD LIMIT ON EVERYTHING ABOVE: **there is zero observational constraint on the surface topography or tectonic pattern of ANY super-Earth.** No exoplanet surface has been resolved. The nearest thing to data is LHS 3844b's thermal phase curve (bare rock, ~1000 K day/night contrast), which constrains the ATMOSPHERE, not the tectonics — the tectonic inference layered on top is model output. Every relief and plate-pattern decision the engine makes at R > 1 is extrapolation from Solar System bodies at g ≤ 1 plus numerical convection models that disagree with each other.

findings.claim: The brief's assumed g(R) exponent is backwards. At fixed composition M ∝ R^3.7 (Zeng et al. 2016, R ∝ M^(1/3.7)), so g = M/R² ∝ R^1.70 — NOT R^0.5–1.0. Compression makes big planets denser, so R grows slower than M^(1/3) and g rises FASTER than linearly. a = 1 is the incompressible LOWER bound, not the upper. Valencia et al. 2007's independent models (g ∝ M^0.50, R ∝ M^0.27) give a = 1.85. Defensible bracket: a ∈ [1.70, 1.85]; use 1.70.

findings.claim: LOAD-BEARING RESULT: in the mobile-lid branch, plate size scales linearly with planet radius and plate COUNT is essentially invariant. Valencia et al. 2007 state it directly: L/R = 0.29 at 1 M_E rising only to 0.30 at 10 M_E. Their Table 1 gives plate length L = 1800 km at 1 M_E with L ∝ M^0.28; combined with R ∝ M^0.27 this is L/R ∝ M^0.01. Plate count N ≈ 4πR²/L² ∝ (L/R)^−2 ∝ R^−0.07 — 5% fewer plates at R = 2, 8% fewer at R = 3. A fixed-N spherical Voronoi whose cells scale with the body is therefore the correct construction, not a placeholder.

findings.claim: The controversy is real and unresolved as of 2024. Valencia et al. 2007 argue plate tectonics is INEVITABLE on super-Earths (thinner plates + larger driving stress: δ ∝ M^−0.45 while normal stress σ ∝ M^1.00). O'Neill & Lenardic 2007 argue the opposite — 'simply increasing planetary radius acts to decrease the ratio of driving to resisting stresses, and thus super-sized Earths are likely to be in an episodic or stagnant lid regime' — and say the effect STRENGTHENS when gravity is included, because Byerlee fault strength (τ_y = C₀ + μP, μ = 0.2) grows with lithostatic pressure faster than buoyancy grows. Korenaga 2010 says size barely matters and water controls everything.

findings.claim: O'Neill & Lenardic's stagnation threshold is startlingly LOW, which is why the disagreement matters for a game that generates R = 1–3 bodies. Verbatim: 'For strong lithospheric strengths, the system may shift from active to stagnant behaviour for a marginally larger planet than Earth. For a range of weaker lithospheres … the stagnation of the lithosphere delayed until quite large planet sizes (scaling factor ~1.10).' Taken at face value their models put the mobile→episodic→stagnant transition between 1.0 and ~1.1 Earth radii — i.e. essentially NO super-Earth is mobile-lid. This is the most aggressive position in the literature and should be treated as one end of the bracket, not as the answer.

findings.claim: Korenaga's position — the one that best survives the last 15 years — is that the controlling variable is surface WATER, not size: 'the planetary size plays a rather minor role and … the likelihood of plate tectonics is controlled largely by the presence of surface water,' because water raises pore fluid pressure and lowers effective friction, the only viable route to weakening the top thermal boundary layer. Valencia et al. independently support the water lever from the other direction: they note hydration halving the plate's yield strength on a 1 M_E planet is equivalent to DOUBLING the planet's mass. Both camps agree water is a strong lever; they disagree on the sign and size of the radius lever. That asymmetry is the practical design guidance.

findings.claim: NOTHING in the retrieved literature predicts MORE, SMALLER plates on a larger planet. Where 3D compressible models keep the lid mobile, the planform gets LONGER-wavelength: Tackley et al. 2013 — 'Convection in large super-Earths is characterised by large upwellings (even with zero basal heating) and small, time-dependent downwellings, which for large super-Earths merge into broad downwellings.' Meier et al. 2021 and 2024 recover degree-1 HEMISPHERIC tectonics (one downwelling hemisphere, one upwelling hemisphere) for super-Earths under a strong lithosphere. So the honest high-R limit is FEWER, BIGGER domains — toward degree-1/2 — not a finer mosaic.

Lichtenberg & Miguel 2024 list the whole debate (Valencia 2007a,c; O'Neill & Lenardic 2007; Kite 2009; Korenaga 2010; Karato 2011; van Heck & Tackley 2011; Stamenković 2012; Foley 2012; Lenardic & Crowley 2012; Tackley 2013; Noack & Breuer 2014; Weller & Lenardic 2016; O'Neill 2016) and conclude they are 'not reaching convergence (Lenardic 2018).' They add the Solar-System prior: 'Earth is the only planet that undergoes mobile lid tectonics at present day … Therefore, stagnant lid geodynamics may be a better approximation for exoplanets.'

The nearest datum is LHS 3844b's thermal phase curve (bare rock, ~1040 K day / ~0 K night, ~1000 K contrast), which constrains the ATMOSPHERE; the hemispheric-tectonics result layered on it is model output. findings.claim: What distinguishes the regimes VISUALLY — the renderer's real contract. MOBILE: a global connected network of narrow linear belts partitioning the sphere into ~7–15 plates, relief concentrated at boundaries (convergent ranges / divergent rifts / transform offsets), flat cratonic interiors, crater record erased. STAGNANT: no global boundary network at all — ancient crater size-frequency distribution + discrete volcanic constructs (shields, calderas, coronae, tessera) + long-wavelength dynamic topography + isolated graben systems; structurally SPARSE and patch/point-dominated. EPISODIC: stagnant character overprinted by globally-synchronous resurfacing, giving sharp-edged patchworks of very-young and very-old terrain. Lichtenberg & Miguel's Figure 11 sets out exactly this A1/A2/A3 taxonomy plus the newer plume-lid / squishy-lid and heat-pipe regimes.

findings.claim: Plate size on Earth is set by SLAB SPACING — a lithosphere/mantle-depth scale — not by planet radius directly. Mallard et al. 2016 show Earth's plate size-frequency distribution (seven large plates of similar size plus a fractal tail of small ones) is reproduced when subduction geometry sets the layout: spacing between subducting slabs fixes the large-plate scale, and trench-bending stresses fragment plates into the small tail. This is the MECHANISM behind Law B and it tells you what to vary: since mantle depth D ∝ M^0.28 ∝ R^1.04 (Valencia et al. 2007 §2.2, D = D_E(M/M_E)^0.28), the slab-spacing scale grows essentially in proportion to R — which is exactly why the plate COUNT stays put. It also predicts the small-plate tail should be fractal, i.e. the Voronoi should be size-heterogeneous, not near-uniform.

lenses.contested:
THE DISAGREEMENT IS REAL, LOAD-BEARING, AND STILL OPEN. Do not let the deliverable paper over it.

1. THE SIGN OF ∂P(mobile)/∂R IS UNRESOLVED. Valencia, O'Connell & Sasselov 2007 and O'Neill & Lenardic 2007 were published within months of each other, model the same physics, and reach OPPOSITE conclusions. Both are still cited as live positions in a 2024 Treatise on Geochemistry review, which states in as many words that the models are "not reaching convergence."

2. WHY THEY DISAGREE — the mechanism split is clean and worth encoding as the uncertainty axis:
   • Valencia's chain: bigger planet → higher Ra → more vigorous convection → THINNER lithosphere (δ ∝ M^−0.45) and FASTER flow (u ∝ M^1.19) → larger driving normal stress (σ ∝ M^1.00) → subduction is easier. Driving stress wins.
   • O'Neill & Lenardic's chain: bigger planet → deeper mantle → the depth scale d in τ ≈ ηv/d grows, mitigating the stress rise; meanwhile higher gravity raises lithostatic pressure, and under Byerlee friction (τ_y = C₀ + μP) fault strength grows FASTER than buoyancy. Resisting stress wins. They state explicitly that adding gravity STRENGTHENS their conclusion, which is the direct inverse of Valencia's expectation.
   • Korenaga 2010 rejects the framing: the boundary-layer weakening that matters cannot come from size at all, only from water lowering effective friction — so size is a minor term either way.
   Whether the depth scale d in the convective-stress denominator should grow with the planet is, as far as I can see from what I retrieved, the crux — and it is a modelling choice, not a measurement.

3. WHAT HAS ACTUALLY BEEN SETTLED SINCE 2007 — very little on the headline question, but three things have firmed up:
   (a) Water/volatiles is a lever everyone accepts. Valencia themselves compute that halving yield strength by hydration ≈ doubling planetary mass. So water and size are partially degenerate in the models, which is part of why size alone cannot be pinned down.
   (b) The high-mass PLANFORM lengthens rather than fragments. Tackley et al. 2013 (compressible, DFT post-perovskite rheology) and Meier et al. 2021/2024 (3D, hemispheric) both give broad merged downwellings or degree-1 convection at high mass. Nobody gets a finer plate mosaic. That is the one directional statement I would call reasonably safe.
   (c) The Solar-System prior is one-sided: every non-Earth terrestrial body is stagnant-lid or episodic. Lichtenberg & Miguel 2024 argue stagnant-lid is therefore the better default for exoplanets. But the sample has exactly one mobile-lid member and no members above 1 R_E, so it constrains the small end and says nothing about super-Earths.

4. WHERE I AM DELIBERATELY NOT PAPERING OVER A GAP IN MY OWN RETRIEVAL: I could not load the abstracts of van Heck & Tackley 2011, Foley et al. 2012, Stamenković et al. 2012, or Mallard et al. 2016 (publisher paywalls / elided abstracts / a dead TLS cert on the ETH mirror). Their titles, authors, years and DOIs are verified; their internal reasoning is not, from this run. Law A and Law B rest ONLY on Valencia et al. 2007 and Zeng et al. 2016, both of which I read in full. Law C's bracket rests on Valencia 2007, O'Neill & Lenardic 2007, Korenaga 2010 and Lichtenberg & Miguel 2024 — all fully retrieved. The paywalled four are context, not load-bearing.

5. THE HONEST BOTTOM LINE FOR THE BUILD. The regime question (Law C) is contested and should be encoded as a seeded, water/temperature-dominated draw with a weak sign-ambiguous radius term. The PATTERN question (Law B) is NOT meaningfully contested and is the one the game actually needs: within the mobile-lid branch, plate count is invariant in R and plate size scales with R. The existing fixed-N Voronoi is right; discarding it at large radius via a display-scale bake crossover is the defect, and it is a rendering decision masquerading as a geodynamic one.

lenses.lens:
Relief AMPLITUDE vs planet size — how much total topographic relief a terrestrial planet carries as a function of radius/gravity, and what the codebase's reliefEnvelope() g^-0.58 does when extrapolated above g = 1.

HEADLINE: the codebase's law is not wrong for the Solar System — it is an accidental re-encoding of "absolute relief in km is roughly constant" (which IS what the g<1 sample shows), and that is precisely the property that must NOT be extrapolated. Extrapolated to super-Earths it predicts absolute relief GROWING with planet size (19.8 km at 1 R⊕ → 26.5 km at 2 R⊕), which contradicts four independent physical arguments that all say relief must FALL as ~1/g above Earth gravity.

AUDIT FINDING 1 — the brief's premise about the mass-radius exponent is backwards. The brief says "realistic compression softens the exponent (a ≈ 0.5–1.0)". Compression STEEPENS it. Constant density gives M ∝ R³ ⇒ g ∝ R¹. Self-compression makes big planets DENSER, so M ∝ R^3.7 ⇒ g ∝ R^1.70. Zeng, Sasselov & Jacobsen (2016), retrieved: R/R⊕ = (1.07 − 0.21·CMF)·(M/M⊕)^(1/3.7), valid 1–8 M⊕. At CMF = 0.33 this gives a = dln g/dln R = 1.700, constant to 3 decimals across R = 1.0–2.0. A 1.5 R⊕ planet is 4.5 M⊕ and 1.99 g, not 1.5 g. Everything downstream inherits this.

AUDIT FINDING 2 — the codebase's own gravity derivation contradicts that. body-condition-vector.js:37 sets surfaceGravity = g_c·(R/R_c), and its comment states the assumption explicitly: "M_derived(R) = M_c·(R/R_c)³ ⇒ g = g_c·(R/R_c)". That is constant density, i.e. g ∝ R^1.0. So the lab under-reads a 1.6 R⊕ super-Earth's gravity by 39% (1.60 vs 2.22). This matters more than the relief exponent itself, because g feeds tectonics, magmatism, crater scaling and the relief envelope alike. Fix it once at the source or every downstream exponent has to be pre-distorted to compensate.

AUDIT FINDING 3 — g is a poor independent variable below 1 g, and that is why the anchor fit landed where it did. Mercury and Mars have effectively identical surface gravity (0.377 vs 0.378) and relief differing by 3.05× (9.85 vs 30.0 km). Over Earth/Venus/Mars/Mercury/Moon, a free-intercept log-log fit gives ln(range_km) vs ln g slope = −0.068, r² = 0.015 — i.e. absolute relief is statistically UNCORRELATED with gravity in the observed sample. Drop Venus (my weakest number) and it is slope +0.004, r² = 0.000. All of the apparent relief/R trend (slope −0.81, r² = 0.80) is carried by 1/R alone. The Q_RELIEF = 0.58 fit is therefore a radius proxy dressed as a gravity law; it has no predictive content in g, and running it past its anchors is unconstrained.

AUDIT FINDING 4 — RELIEF_FLOOR = 0.40 lands inside the super-Earth range under the corrected exponent. The code's comment says it "binds only g ≳ 4.85", true at Q = 0.58. At Q = 1.588 it binds at g = 1.78, i.e. R = 1.40 R⊕, M = 3.4 M⊕ — the middle of the population the directive is about. It would clamp the entire super-Earth branch flat. It must fall to ≈0.12 (covers to R ≈ 2.2 R⊕) or be removed. It was never derived; the comment says it was "inherited from the reliefGravityFactor floor".

MEASURED BASELINE (consistent measure: total dynamic range, max minus min elevation — NOT RMS; see below):
  Earth   R=6371km  g=1.000  19.78 km  relief/R=3.11e-3  (1.00× Earth)
  Venus   R=6052    g=0.904  ~14.6 km  2.42e-3  (0.78×)  [weakest source — see findings]
  Mars    R=3390    g=0.378  30.0 km   8.85e-3  (2.85×)
  Mercury R=2440    g=0.377   9.85 km  4.04e-3  (1.30×)  [N. hemisphere, Zuber+2012]
  Moon    R=1737    g=0.165  19.9 km   1.15e-2  (3.69×)
  Io      R=1822    g=0.183  ~17.5 km  9.61e-3  (3.09×)  [unverified, excluded from fits]

THE STANDARD STRENGTH LIMIT, stated properly. Melosh (2011) Ch.3, retrieved, eq. 3.17: Δh ≈ (3/2π)·Y/(G·ρ̄·ρ_c·R̄), which is identically Δh = 2Y/(ρ_c·g) since g = (4/3)πGρ̄R̄. Guimond+2022 eq. 21 writes the same force balance as Y ≈ 0.5·ρ_c·g·h. ASSUMPTIONS, all of which matter: (i) Jeffreys' (1929) flat-Earth elastic stress distribution — the deviatoric stress a distance ~w/4 below a load of width w is ~1/2 to 1/3 of ρgh; (ii) holds only for loads of horizontal scale ≲ a few hundred km, so it caps MOUNTAINS, not the planetary-scale dichotomies and ocean basins that dominate Mars's and Earth's dynamic range; (iii) ideal-plastic yield at a single Y, no depth dependence, no temperature dependence, no pore fluid; (iv) g constant over the height of the load; (v) ρ_c uniform. Melosh's own arithmetic: Δh_Earth(m) ≈ 80.4·Y(MPa), so Y = 100 MPa (crushing strength of granite) gives 8 km — Everest. Guimond et al. (2026, Space Sci Rev review) endorse the ceiling as "Earth-size planets likely do not support mountains surpassing 10 km".

AND THE TEXTBOOK ITSELF SAYS IT IS ONLY A CEILING. Melosh, verbatim: "if Y is the same for all the terrestrial planets, we should expect 8 km high mountains on Venus, 24 km high mountains on Mars and 50 km high mountains on the Moon... this is not far off for Venus and Mars, but is more than twice the observed topographic range on the Moon. Evidently strength is not the major factor limiting the Moon's topography: History must play a role, too." This is the whole shape of the answer: relief = min(what the processes actually build, what gravity will tolerate). Below ~1 g the process supply is the binding constraint and it does not track g at all (r² = 0.015). At and above ~1 g the ceiling comes down onto the supply and takes over. That is a BREAK at g ≈ 1, not a single power law — which is exactly the question the brief asked and exactly where the current code is unconstrained.

FOUR INDEPENDENT ARGUMENTS, ALL CONVERGING ON h_km ∝ g^-1 ABOVE 1 g:
 (1) Crustal strength (Jeffreys/Melosh): h = 2Y/(ρ_c g) ⇒ exactly g^-1 by construction.
 (2) Dynamic topography from stagnant-lid convection (Guimond, Rudge & Shorttle 2022, 2D temperature-dependent-viscosity convection + 1D thermal evolution): h_peak ∝ h_rms ∝ M^-0.5 for dry olivine at solar U/Th. Converting with g ∝ M^0.4595 (from Zeng+2016): h ∝ g^-1.09. Their cold and hot bounds are M^-0.34 and M^-0.74 ⇒ g^-0.74 to g^-1.61.
 (3) Isostatic relief from crustal thickness contrast (Kite, Manga & Gaidos 2009, verbatim): "the thickness contrast between continental and oceanic crust will scale as the inverse of gravity... because crustal thickness variations are limited by crustal flow (and brittle failure down gravitational-potential-energy gradients)". Same paper: "the absolute thickness of the crust also scales as the inverse of gravity".
 (4) The basalt→eclogite phase transition caps basaltic crustal thickness at a fixed PRESSURE, so the depth ⇒ thickness ⇒ isostatic relief all go as 1/g (Guimond+2022, citing Jull & Arkani-Hamed 1995; ~15 km peak isostatic relief for a Venus-like case).
Two of these (2, 3) come from opposite tectonic regimes — stagnant lid and plate tectonics — and land on the same exponent. That robustness is the strongest thing in this report.

IS A SINGLE POWER LAW IN g THE RIGHT FORM ABOVE g = 1? Above g = 1, yes: four mechanisms agree on ~g^-1 and no retrieved source predicts a regime change in 1 < g < 3. Across g = 1, no: a single global law is provably wrong in both directions. Fitting Q = 1.59 down through the Solar System anchors predicts 67 km of relief on the Moon (observed 19.9). Fitting Q = 0.58 up predicts absolute relief RISING with planet mass. The break is physical, not cosmetic.

DOES ANYTHING CHANGE THE EXPONENT ABOVE 1 g? Three candidates, none quantified in anything I retrieved: (a) Y itself may depend on g — Guimond+2022 flag that "surface gravity has a nonlinear effect on brittle strength through its influence on porosity and fracture density (Heap et al. 2017)"; if Y rises with g the exponent is shallower than 1. (b) Byrne et al. (2021) "eggshell planets" — worlds whose brittle lithosphere is ≲5 km thick have "little elevated topography" at all; these are super-Earths that are hot, young, or radiogenically rich, i.e. a SEPARATE COLLAPSE MODE not captured by any smooth power law. (c) Erosion — the Guimond+2026 review notes erosion "grinds down mountains" over 100-Myr timescales but gives no scaling with g. I would not encode any of these.

OBSERVATIONAL CONSTRAINT ON SUPER-EARTH TOPOGRAPHY: none. Zero. Every number above g = 1 is modelled. McTier & Kipping (2018) assess whether exotopography could EVER be detected and conclude it needs Colossus/OWL-class telescopes and a Mars-sized planet transiting a white dwarf; they explicitly frame it as a question for "the coming decades". Byrne et al. (2021) offer their eggshell prediction as something that "can be tested with future generations of telescopes". Nobody has measured a mountain outside the Solar System. Anything the game does above 1 g is a defensible physical extrapolation, never a calibration.

ABSOLUTE km vs relief/R — WHICH I AM REPORTING (brief item 5). The physics is clean in ABSOLUTE km; relief/R is the code's variable and carries an extra 1/R. Because R ∝ g^(1/a) = g^0.588, the two exponents differ by exactly 1/a = 0.588: h_km ∝ g^-q ⟺ relief/R ∝ g^-(q + 0.588). All Q values I quote below are for relief/R, matching the code. The corresponding absolute exponent is always Q − 0.588.

DYNAMIC RANGE vs RMS — they behave differently and must not be mixed (brief item 2). Every number in my table is total dynamic range (max − min), which is what the code's anchors already encode (Earth target 0.003 × 6371 = 19 km = Everest + Challenger Deep). Dynamic range is set by the single most extreme feature and so is dominated by one-offs — Mars's 30 km IS Tharsis plus Hellas, and Zuber+2012 note that removing Tharsis/Valles Marineris drops Mars to roughly Mercury's range. RMS is a bulk statistic and is far smaller and far better behaved: >90% of Venus lies within −1.0 to +2.5 km. Guimond+2022 model RMS dynamic topography of HUNDREDS OF METRES for Earth-mass planets and say so plainly. DO NOT import their absolute amplitudes — they state their own model gives ocean-basin capacities <1 Earth ocean where Venus/Earth/Mars observe 3.4/3.3/2.9. Their EXPONENT is the trustworthy product; their PREFACTOR is not. Normalise to Earth, which the code already does.

lenses.law:
DEFINITIONS
  R      planet radius in Earth radii
  g      surface gravity in Earth g
  a      mass–radius gravity exponent, g = R^a. a = 1.700 (Zeng+2016, CMF = 0.33, constant to 3 d.p. over R = 1–2)
  h(g)   total topographic dynamic range (max − min elevation) in km
  h_⊕    Earth anchor = 19.8 km dynamic range (peak-prominence anchor if wanted instead: 8–10 km)
  E(g)   the code's reliefEnvelope multiplier: relief/R normalised so Earth = 1

ABSOLUTE FORM (where the physics lives):
      h(g) = h_⊕ · min(1, g)^(−q),      q = 1.0  (+0.6 / −0.3)
  i.e. h = h_⊕ for g ≤ 1 (process/history-limited, NOT gravity-limited)
       h = h_⊕ / g for g > 1 (strength- and convection-limited)
  Hard physical ceiling, never to be exceeded at any g: h ≤ 2Y/(ρ_c·g·9.81) with Y ≈ 100–200 MPa,
  ρ_c = 2700 kg/m³ ⇒ 7.6–15.1 km at 1 g, 3.8–7.6 km at 2 g, 2.5–5.0 km at 3 g.

CODE FORM (relief/R, normalised Earth = 1 — drop-in for reliefEnvelope):
      E(g) = g^(−Q_lo)   for g ≤ 1     Q_lo = 0.58   (KEEP — empirical, descriptive, see caveat)
      E(g) = g^(−Q_hi)   for g >  1     Q_hi = q + 1/a = 1.0 + 0.588 = 1.588  ≈ 1.59  (+0.6 / −0.3)
  Continuous at g = 1 (both branches = 1). Monotone non-increasing in g everywhere.
      RELIEF_FLOOR: 0.40 → 0.12    (0.40 binds at R = 1.40 R⊕ under Q_hi = 1.588 and would flatten
                                    the whole super-Earth branch; 0.12 binds only beyond R ≈ 2.2 R⊕)
      RELIEF_CEIL:  133 — unchanged, still never binds.

  Q_lo IS NOT PHYSICS. It is a radius proxy: over the anchor set, absolute relief is uncorrelated with g
  (slope −0.07, r² = 0.015) and all the relief/R signal is 1/R. It is fine as a descriptive device for
  g ≤ 1 because the game already draws those bodies inside the calibrated range. Rename it or comment it
  so nobody extrapolates it again. Do not "smooth" the two branches into one exponent.

⚠ UNIT WARNING — THIS IS THE PART THAT WILL SILENTLY BREAK. Q_hi = 1.588 is correct ONLY if the g handed
to reliefEnvelope is true self-compressed gravity, g = R^1.70. The lab currently supplies constant-density
gravity, g_lab = g_c·(R/R_c) ∝ R^1.0 (body-condition-vector.js:37, assumption stated in its own comment).
Pick exactly one:
  (A) PREFERRED — fix the source: surfaceGravity = g_c·(R/R_c)^1.70, then use Q_hi = 1.588.
      This also corrects tectonics, magmatism and crater scaling, which read the same g.
  (B) leave g_lab alone and use Q_hi = a + q = 2.700 in reliefEnvelope only.
  Do not mix. Both encode identical physics; (B) hides a wrong g everywhere else.

RADIUS FORM (invariant to the g bug — the safest thing to bake if you want one line that cannot rot):
      relief/R ∝ R^(−2.70)   for R > 1        (equivalently h_km ∝ R^(−1.70))
      relief/R ∝ R^(−1.00)   for R ≤ 1        (equivalently h_km ≈ constant)

WHERE Q_hi = 1.588 COMES FROM, in one line: relief/R = h/R; h ∝ g^-1 (four independent mechanisms);
R = g^(1/1.700) = g^0.588; therefore relief/R ∝ g^(−1 − 0.588) = g^−1.588.

CROSS-CHECK, AND THE REASON I TRUST THIS: the strength-limit route gives Q_hi = 1.588. Guimond+2022's
completely independent convection route (h ∝ M^−0.5, converted through g ∝ M^0.4595) gives Q_hi = 1.68.
Those agree to 5% having shared no assumptions beyond the mass–radius relation.

UNCERTAINTY ON Q_hi, honestly: the ±band is Guimond+2022's cold-to-hot interior bracket, Q_hi ∈ [1.33, 2.20]
(their M^−0.34 to M^−0.74). The strength argument pins q = 1 exactly by construction, so 1.588 is the point
of maximum agreement rather than the centre of a measured distribution. Any Q_hi in 1.3–2.2 is defensible;
0.58 is not, and neither is anything below ~1.1, because that would require absolute relief to be nearly
independent of gravity in a regime where the strength ceiling is demonstrably binding.

FROM THE PREFACTOR, NOT THE EXPONENT — the one caveat that could move the whole curve: Y is uncertain by
5× (100 MPa granite crushing strength → 7.6 km on Earth; ~500 MPa brittle-ductile maximum, Katayama 2021 via
Guimond+2022 → 37.8 km). This scales h everywhere and cancels completely in the Earth-normalised E(g). It is
the reason to keep normalising to Earth rather than computing km from Y.
lenses.validityRange:
MEASURED — the g ≤ 1 branch, 0.165 ≤ g ≤ 1.0 (Moon → Earth), 1737 ≤ R_km ≤ 6371. Six bodies, all at or below Earth gravity. The finding here is negative and robust: absolute relief is 10–30 km and statistically uncorrelated with g (slope −0.068, r² = 0.015; −0.004, r² = 0.000 without Venus), with a 3.05× spread at fixed g (Mercury 9.85 km vs Mars 30.0 km, both at 0.377–0.378 g). Q_lo is a fit to R, not to g. Its formal validity is only over the anchor set; the code already respects that.

STANDARD THEORY — the strength ceiling h = 2Y/(ρ_c g) is derivable at any g (Jeffreys 1929 → Melosh 2011). But it only BINDS where the process supply would otherwise exceed it. Melosh shows explicitly that it over-predicts the Moon by >2× and, in his words, gives "ridiculous conclusions" for bodies like Phobos. Treat it as a ceiling above 1 g and as inactive below.

MODELLED, DEFENSIBLE — 1 < g ≤ 2.2, i.e. 1.0 < R ≤ 1.6 R⊕, 1.0 < M ≤ 5.7 M⊕. This is the interval where every ingredient is inside its own stated validity: Zeng+2016 M–R is quoted for 1–8 M⊕; Guimond+2022 ran 0.1–5 M⊕ and note their own eq. (7) extrapolates equations of state beyond validity (though only 1.2% radius error at 5 M⊕ vs Hakim+2018); Rogers (2015)'s ~1.6 R⊕ rocky/sub-Neptune boundary is the physical top of the population. Q_hi = 1.588 is supported here by four independent mechanisms. This is where the directive's "super-Earths" actually live and where I would ship the law.

EXTRAPOLATION — 2.2 < g ≤ 3.3, i.e. 1.6 < R ≤ 2.0 R⊕, 5.7 < M ≤ 13 M⊕. Nothing forbids the law, but bodies here are probably not rocky at all, and Kite+2009 warn that pMELTS-class melting models are uncalibrated above 3 GPa / 1460 °C exactly in this range. Physically plausible, observationally void, and the population is largely fictional.

PURE SPECULATION — g > 3.3 (R > 2 R⊕). Use the floor and stop reasoning. No source I retrieved models topography there.

NO OBSERVATIONAL CONSTRAINT ANYWHERE ABOVE g = 1. Not weak constraint — none. No exoplanet topography has been measured. McTier & Kipping (2018) find that even detecting it requires Colossus/OWL-class apertures and a Mars-sized planet transiting a white dwarf, and that the method is "unproductive" for planets around Sun-like or M-dwarf stars. Byrne et al. (2021) offer the eggshell-planet flatness prediction as a test for "future generations of telescopes". So: the g ≤ 1 branch is calibration; the g > 1 branch is derivation. They should not be presented to the player, or in the code comments, as the same kind of thing.

REGIME ESCAPE THAT THE LAW DOES NOT COVER — Byrne et al. (2021) "eggshell planets": super-Earths that are young, hot, close-in, or radiogenically rich can have a brittle lithosphere ≲5 km thick and essentially NO elevated topography, at any gravity. That is a discrete collapse, not a point on this curve. If the world engine already has a lithosphere/surface-temperature driver, that is the correct place to express it — as a separate multiplicative kill switch, not by bending Q_hi.

findings.claim: The brief's stated premise is backwards: self-compression STEEPENS the gravity-radius exponent, it does not soften it. Constant density gives g ∝ R^1.0; realistic rocky interiors give g ∝ R^1.70. Zeng, Sasselov & Jacobsen (2016) give R/R⊕ = (1.07 − 0.21·CMF)·(M/M⊕)^(1/3.7), valid 1–8 M⊕, CMF 0–0.4. At CMF = 0.33 this yields a = dln g/dln R = 1.700, constant to three decimals over R = 1.0–2.0. A 1.5 R⊕ planet is 4.47 M⊕ and 1.99 g, not 1.5 g. This propagates into every downstream exponent.

findings.claim: The standard crustal-strength limit is Δh = 2Y/(ρ_c·g), equivalently Melosh eq. 3.17: Δh ≈ (3/2π)·Y/(G·ρ̄·ρ_c·R̄), and Guimond+2022 eq. 21: Y ≈ 0.5·ρ_c·g·h. It rests on Jeffreys' (1929) flat-Earth elastic stress result that a load of width w drives a deviatoric stress of ~ρgh/2 to ρgh/3 at depth ~w/4, and therefore holds only for loads narrower than a few hundred km — it caps MOUNTAINS, not planetary-scale dichotomies or ocean basins. Melosh's arithmetic: Δh_Earth(m) ≈ 80.4·Y(MPa), so Y = 100 MPa (granite crushing strength) gives 8 km ≈ Everest.

findings.claim: THE LOAD-BEARING QUALIFICATION, and Melosh says it himself: the strength limit is a CEILING that low-gravity bodies do not reach. Evidently strength is not the major factor limiting the Moon's topography: History must play a role, too.' He adds that for small bodies like Phobos the limit 'leads to ridiculous conclusions'. This is why relief = min(process supply, strength ceiling), and why the correct functional form has a BREAK near g = 1 rather than a single exponent.

findings.claim: A third and fourth independent ∝1/g route, from the crust rather than the mantle or the mountain. This is because crustal thickness variations are limited by crustal flow (and brittle failure down gravitational-potential-energy gradients).' Same paper: 'the absolute thickness of the crust also scales as the inverse of gravity' (higher g moves the solidus and suppresses melting). Separately, the basalt→eclogite transition occurs at fixed PRESSURE, so its depth — and hence maximum basaltic crustal thickness and the isostatic relief it supports — also goes as 1/g; this caps peak isostatic relief near 15 km for a Venus-like case. Note routes (2) and (3) come from opposite tectonic regimes (stagnant lid vs plate tectonics) and give the same exponent, which is why I trust the law across the unresolved tectonics debate.

findings.claim: Dynamic range and RMS behave differently and must not be interchanged. All my table values are total dynamic range (max − min), matching the code's existing anchors (Earth 0.003 × 6371 km = 19 km = Everest + Challenger Deep). Dynamic range is set by single extreme features and is therefore history-dominated — Zuber+2012 note that removing Tharsis and Valles Marineris drops Mars's remaining range to roughly the Hellas rim-to-floor depth, comparable to Mercury's. RMS is far smaller and better behaved: >90% of Venus lies within −1.0 to +2.5 km, and Guimond+2022 model RMS dynamic topography of merely HUNDREDS OF METRES for Earth-mass planets. Do not import their absolute amplitudes: they state their model gives ocean-basin capacities <1 Earth ocean where Venus/Earth/Mars observe 3.4/3.3/2.9. Their exponent is the product worth taking; their prefactor is not. Normalising to Earth (as the code already does) is what makes this safe.

lenses.contested:
1. THE BRIEF'S OWN PREMISE IS WRONG, AND IT IS THE BIGGEST CORRECTION HERE. The brief states "realistic compression softens the exponent" and offers a ≈ 0.5–1.0. It steepens it: a = 1.70. This is not a literature dispute — it is a sign error that follows from M ∝ R^3.7 (Zeng+2016). Because a appears twice in the final exponent (once converting h to relief/R, once converting R to g), getting it wrong would have propagated everywhere. Worth flagging back to whoever wrote the brief.

2. TECTONIC REGIME ON SUPER-EARTHS — genuinely unresolved for 18 years, and I am not going to paper over it. Valencia et al. (2007) and van Heck & Tackley (2011) argue plate tectonics is equally or MORE likely on larger planets; O'Neill & Lenardic (2007) argue from convection simulations that increasing radius lowers the driving/resisting stress ratio and that higher gravity locks faults, pushing super-Earths into episodic or stagnant-lid regimes. Neither of the two primary papers cleared a paywall for me (see sources), so I am reporting the dispute's existence from summaries, not adjudicating it. WHY IT DOES NOT SINK THE LAW: my two mechanism-based routes come from OPPOSITE sides of this argument — Guimond+2022's dynamic topography is stagnant-lid, Kite+2009's crustal thickness contrast is plate-tectonic — and both give h ∝ g^-1. So the AMPLITUDE law survives the disagreement. What does NOT survive is the CHARACTER of the terrain: linear orogenic belts and continents versus volcanic edifices and flood plains. If the world engine ever wants to branch terrain STYLE on tectonic mode, that branch is genuinely underdetermined by the science and is a taste call, and should be labelled as one rather than dressed in a citation.

3. THE CRUSTAL YIELD STRENGTH Y IS UNCERTAIN BY 5×, AND THE LITERATURE DOES NOT CONVERGE. 100 MPa (granite crushing strength, Melosh's choice, Guimond's fiducial) gives 7.6 km on Earth. ~500 MPa (brittle-ductile transition maximum, Katayama 2021 via Guimond) gives 37.8 km — Guimond+2022 quote "~40 km" and immediately add "it is a limit not necessarily reached in practice". Guimond+2026 settle on ~10 km. This is a factor-5 spread in the PREFACTOR and it cancels exactly in the Earth-normalised multiplier. It is the single strongest reason to keep normalising to Earth rather than computing kilometres from Y.

4. WHETHER Y ITSELF DEPENDS ON g — unresolved, and it is the one thing that could move the exponent rather than the prefactor. Guimond+2022 note that "surface gravity has a nonlinear effect on brittle strength through its influence on porosity and fracture density (Heap et al. 2017)". If Y rises with g, the true exponent is shallower than 1.0 — plausibly toward the 0.74 cold-interior end of the bracket. Nobody I retrieved has quantified it. It is a real reason not to over-commit to 1.588 to three significant figures.

5. MODELLED AMPLITUDES DISAGREE WITH OBSERVATION BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE, AND THE AUTHORS SAY SO. Guimond+2022's stagnant-lid model gives RMS dynamic topography of hundreds of metres and ocean-basin capacities <1 Earth ocean, where the observed Venus/Earth/Mars values are 3.4/3.3/2.9. Their own words: "The peak and RMS elevations of our terrestrial planets are much higher than those predicted by the dynamic topography scaling here. Other mechanisms contribute to supporting higher topography on planets." Dynamic topography is one contributor among several. Take the exponent; discard the prefactor; normalise to Earth.

6. THE Q_lo BRANCH IS NOT PHYSICS AND I WOULD NOT DEFEND IT AS SUCH. Below g = 1, absolute relief is uncorrelated with g (r² = 0.015), so ANY exponent fitted there is a coincidence of the sample. Q_lo = 0.58 works as a descriptive device because the g<1 draws stay inside the calibration set, but the code comment currently presents it as a "strength-cap exponent", which it is not. That mislabelling is what made the super-Earth extrapolation look sanctioned. Recommend the comment change even if the number does not.

7. WHERE EXACTLY THE BREAK SITS IS SOFT. I place it at g = 1 because that is where Melosh's ceiling stops over-predicting (Venus and Mars sit near it, the Moon does not) and because it makes the law continuous with Earth = 1 for free. But the crossover is a smooth competition between two curves, not a kink, and nothing I retrieved pins it to better than roughly a factor of 1.5 in g. If a kink ever reads badly in-game, softening it with a min() over the two branches or a smooth blend is scientifically neutral — the exponents are the constrained part, the corner is not.

8. FINALLY, THE HONEST TOP-LEVEL CAVEAT. This is derivation, not calibration. Every anchor in the codebase is at or below Earth gravity; the entire super-Earth branch rests on four theoretical arguments that agree with each other and on ZERO measurements. That agreement is genuinely reassuring — four mechanisms from three different subfields converging on g^-1 is about as good as unobserved physics gets — but it is not the same kind of knowledge as the g<1 anchors, and the code comment should not let a future reader mistake one for the other.

lenses.lens: Horizontal WAVELENGTH / feature scale vs planet size (R), for the Well Dipper world engine's km-keyed `featureSizeKm` knobs.
lenses.law:
THERE IS NO SINGLE WAVELENGTH EXPONENT. Terrestrial topography carries FIVE wavelength families with FIVE different R-dependences, and blending them into one number destroys the physics. Deliver them separately.

═══ MASTER FORM ═══
For feature class k:   λ_k(R) = λ_k,⊕ · R^(p_k)      [λ in km, R in Earth radii]
Angular (what the renderer sees):  θ_k = λ_k /(R·6371) ∝ R^(p_k − 1)
Code hook: `featureFrequencyFromKm(R, L_km, c) = c·R·6371/L_km` is already correct — so a FIXED
`featureSizeKm` silently encodes p=0. Only families A and B need `featureSizeKm ∝ R^p` with p>0.

═══ THE GRAVITY BRIDGE (must be fixed first — the brief's premise is inverted) ═══
The brief says "g = g_E·R^a with a ≈ 0.5–1.0 … compression softens the exponent." That is BACKWARDS.
Compression makes a planet SMALLER for given mass, so g rises FASTER with R, not slower.
  R ∝ M^β with β = 0.262–0.272 (Valencia et al. 2006, 2007)  ⇒  g = M/R² ∝ R^(1/β − 2)
  g(R) = R^1.00              for R ≤ 1   (uncompressed; g = (4/3)πGρR at fixed ρ)
  g(R) = R^(1.75 ± 0.07)     for 1 ≤ R ≤ 1.9   [β=0.272 → 1.68 ; β=0.262 → 1.82]
Constant density (β=1/3) gives exactly R^1.0 — that is the FLOOR of the exponent, not the ceiling.
Note the codebase's `deriveConditionVector` uses g = g_c·(R/R_c), i.e. a=1.0. That is right below
1 R_⊕ and understates g by 1.7× at R=2 (predicts 2.0 g, physics says 3.4 g). Everything downstream
that reads g — including Q_RELIEF — inherits that error.

═══ FAMILY A — GEOMETRIC / DEEP-MANTLE ═══  (hemispheric dichotomies, superplume provinces,
continent-scale highlands, largest multi-ring basins)
  λ_A = 2π·R_km / √(l(l+1)),  l = 1–2      [Jeans relation, Wieczorek 2007 eq. after eq.5]
       l=1 → 4.443·R_km ;  l=2 → 2.565·R_km
  λ_A,⊕ = 16,300–28,300 km       p_A = +1.00 EXACTLY      θ_A ∝ R^0 (constant fraction of the disc)
  Why l=1–2: planetary topography spectra are red (Kaula-like), so power always peaks at the lowest
  degrees; and spherical-shell mobile-lid convection self-selects degree-1 or degree-2 planform.
  This is the only exponent in the whole table with zero uncertainty — it is sphere geometry.
  ⚠ DEGREE vs WAVELENGTH: degree l is dimensionless and does NOT scale with R; physical wavelength
  at fixed l scales EXACTLY ∝ R. Report wavelength; never port a degree number as if it were a km.

═══ FAMILY B — CONVECTIVE CELL / PLATE / SLAB SPACING ═══  (tectonic provinces, orogenic belt
spacing, rift spacing, plate outlines)
  λ_B = A_c · d_mantle,   A_c ∈ [2, 6]      d_mantle(⊕) = 2890 km
  d_mantle ∝ R^1.10 (bracket 1.05–1.20)   [Valencia 2006 Table 1: D ∝ M^0.286–0.316, R ∝ M^0.263–0.272]
  λ_B,⊕ ≈ 5,800 km (A_c=2, Rayleigh–Bénard rigid-rigid onset) … 16,300 km (A_c=5.65, Earth's observed
  degree-2 = 5.65·d) — cells are far wider than onset because low-viscosity channels and continents
  push mantle flow to long wavelength.
  p_B = +1.10 ± 0.15        θ_B ∝ R^+0.10 (essentially constant on the disc)
  Empirical plate-size check: the plate-area distribution is a power law with cumulative exponent
  0.25 ± 0.05 expressed in STERADIANS (dimensionless), cut off by the constraint that areas sum to
  4π sr. A dimensionless-on-the-sphere distribution means plate linear size ∝ R exactly — consistent
  with p_B ≈ 1. This is an n=1 sample; treat 1.0–1.1 as one number, not two.

═══ FAMILY C — FLEXURAL / LITHOSPHERIC ═══  (mountain-range width, forebulge & trough spacing,
wrinkle-ridge and graben spacing, the observed roughness scale-break)
  T_e = [Ra_c·κ·η / (ρ·α·ΔT·g)]^(1/3)   ∝ g^(−1/3)   [marginal-stability boundary-layer result;
        STANDARD theory. Independent of mantle depth d — this is why it does not scale with R.]
  λ_flex = 2π·[ E·T_e³ / (3(1−ν²)·Δρ·g) ]^(1/4)   ∝ T_e^(3/4)·g^(−1/4) ∝ g^(−1/2)
  ⇒ p_C = −0.5 × 1.70 = −0.85          θ_C ∝ R^(−1.85)  ← features look ~2× finer on the disc at R=1.5
  Earth anchors (computed): T_e=30 km, E=100 GPa, ν=0.25, Δρ=2300 kg/m³, g=9.81 → flexural parameter
  α = 81 km, λ_flex = 507 km.
  Independent OBSERVED anchor — the topographic scale break:
     Earth 10 km · Mars ~10–20 km · Mercury ~10–20 km · Moon ~10–20 km · VENUS 50 km
  Venus is 0.95 R_⊕ with 5× Earth's break scale. That single fact FALSIFIES "break ∝ R" and confirms
  the break is thermal/rheological (T_e), not geometric.
  ⚠ THIS IS THE CONTESTED FAMILY. Bracket the exponent p_C ∈ [−0.9, 0.0]; use −0.85 only if you
  accept incompressible convection scaling (see `contested`).

═══ FAMILY D — IMPACT ═══
  D1 crater diameter for a fixed impactor (gravity regime):  D ∝ g^(−μ/(2+μ))
      μ = 0.4 (dry sand / regolith / porous) → −0.167 ;  μ = 0.55 (wet + rocky, incl. Hard Rocks) → −0.216
      ⇒ p_D1 = −0.28 … −0.37 in R.
      AUDIT: codebase `K_GS = 0.17` is the DRY-SAND value. A silicate-crust world should use 0.22.
      This is a real, small, defensible fix (`rockyCrust` already exists to switch on).
  D2 simple→complex transition:  D_t = K_DT / g,  K_DT = 3.1 km·g_⊕      p_D2 = −1.70 in R
      AUDIT: CONFIRMED. Lunar transition ≈ 19–20 km × g=0.165 → K = 3.1–3.3. Code's 3.1 is right.
      (Pike 1977's ONSET-of-complex-shapes threshold is lower, D*=10.6 km → K≈1.75; 3.1 corresponds
      to the flat-floor/fully-complex threshold. Both are legitimate; 3.1 is the conservative one.)
      Consequence: R=1.5 → g=2.0 → D_t = 1.6 km ; R=2 → g=3.4 → D_t = 0.9 km. On a super-Earth
      essentially EVERY resolvable crater is complex — central peaks and terraces everywhere, no
      simple bowls. That is the single most visually legible super-Earth prediction in this brief.
      Known offset with a derivable sign: impact velocity v² = v_∞² + v_esc², v_esc ∝ √(gR) ∝ R^1.35,
      so super-Earths impact harder; on Mercury high velocity already pushes the observed onset
      1.5–2× above the pure-1/g prediction. Expect real super-Earth D_t to be 1.5–2× ABOVE 3.1/g.
  D3 crater size-frequency DISTRIBUTION SHAPE: p_D3 = 0.00 EXACTLY. The SFD is a property of the
      impactor population, not the target. Do not scale it with R.

═══ FAMILY E — AEOLIAN ═══
  λ_dune = 53 · L_drag,   L_drag = (ρ_s/ρ_f)·d_grain      [MEASURED over ~5 decades]
  p_E = 0.00 in R AND 0.00 in g. Gravity does not appear.
  Anchors (computed from the law): Earth ρ_s/ρ_f=2200, d=180 µm → λ = 21 m. Mars ρ_f≈0.02 kg/m³,
  d=100 µm → λ = 0.77 km (matches the observed "of order a kilometre" martian dunes).
  ⇒ dune wavelength is a function of ATMOSPHERIC DENSITY and GRAIN SIZE only. A thick-atmosphere
  super-Earth gets FINER dunes than Earth; a thin-atmosphere one gets Mars-scale dunes. Drive
  `duneSizeKm` off atmospheric pressure, never off R.

═══ FAMILY F — FLUVIAL ═══
  λ_valley = (6.4 … 12.7)·L_c,   L_c = (D/K)^(1/(2m+1))     [D = soil-creep diffusivity, K = stream
  incision coefficient, m = drainage-area exponent]
  p_F = 0.00 in R. Neither g nor R appears. L_c is 10–100 m at the five measured sites (λ = 10–1000 m).
  ⇒ drainage texture is set by climate and rock erodibility. On a bigger planet it is unchanged in
  km and therefore FINER on the disc as 1/R.

═══ THE ONE-LINE HEADLINE ═══
Going up in R, only the two mantle-driven families keep pace with the planet. Everything from the
lithosphere outward (flexure, craters, dunes, rivers) is set by a LOCAL physical scale that is
constant or shrinking in km. So a super-Earth reads as a FINER-GRAINED world at the same disc size:
same number of continent-scale provinces, ~2× finer mountain texture, ~1.7× finer crater texture,
1/R finer dunes and drainage — plus a near-total absence of simple bowl craters.
Do NOT model "bigger planet = bigger features."
lenses.validityRange:
MEASURED ANCHOR RANGE (where the law is supported by data):
• g ∈ [0.006, 0.90] g_⊕ and R ∈ [0.03, 1.0] R_⊕. Every real body used anywhere in this analysis
  (Mimas, Phobos, Moon, Mercury, Mars, Venus, Earth) sits AT OR BELOW Earth gravity. This is the same
  defect already flagged in the repo's Q_RELIEF fit — the horizontal-wavelength anchors have it too.
• Aeolian (Family E) is the ONE exception: the 53·L_drag law was tested against a high-pressure CO₂
  wind tunnel reproducing Venus-like conditions and against martian dunes, spanning ~5 decades in
  L_drag. It is the best-constrained item in this brief.
• Fluvial (Family F): five field sites, all terrestrial, all Earth g. Zero off-Earth constraint.
• Crater D_t = 3.1/g: anchored on Moon (0.165 g), Mars/Mercury (0.38 g), Earth (1.0 g). Interpolation
  over ~6× in g. Good.

EXTRAPOLATION BEGINS AT R > 1.0 R_⊕. There is NO observational constraint of any kind on super-Earth
topography — no resolved surface, no altimetry, no shape model. Every p_k above 1 R_⊕ is a physics
extrapolation, and must be labelled as such in the code comment. State this plainly to the owner:
"scientifically predicted for super-Earths" means predicted from Solar-System-calibrated physics,
NOT observed.

THE g(R) BRIDGE ITSELF has a hard validity window:
• g ∝ R^1.75 holds only for 1 ≤ R ≤ 1.9 R_⊕ (= 1–10 M_⊕, the mass range Valencia et al. actually
  computed) AND only for Earth-like Fe/Si with negligible volatiles.
• Below R = 1 use g ∝ R^1.0. The two branches must be joined at R=1 (both give g=1 there, so the
  piecewise form is continuous but has a kink in slope — that is physical, it is the onset of
  significant self-compression).
• Above ~1.9 R_⊕ real planets are overwhelmingly volatile-rich sub-Neptunes, not rocky. If the game
  draws rocky planets above 2 R_⊕ it is already outside the observed population; treat the law as
  frozen at R=2 rather than extrapolating further.
• Add water and β drops (0.244 at 50% H₂O), so an ocean world's g rises even faster with R.

PER-FAMILY CONFIDENCE ORDERING (most to least trustworthy):
A (exact geometry) > E (measured, 5 decades) > D2 (measured, 6× in g) > D1/D3 (lab-measured
π-scaling) > F (measured but Earth-only) > B (modelled, n=1 empirical check) > C (modelled, sign
disputed above ~5 M_⊕).

findings.claim: The brief's premise on the mass-radius exponent is inverted. Compression makes g rise FASTER with radius, not slower: R ∝ M^β with β = 0.267–0.272 for super-Earths gives g = M/R² ∝ R^(1/β−2) = R^1.68–1.75. Constant density (β=1/3) gives exactly R^1.0, which is the FLOOR, not the ceiling. The brief's stated a ≈ 0.5–1.0 is not attainable for any Earth-composition planet above 1 R_⊕.
findings.sourceRef: Valencia, O'Connell & Sasselov 2006, 'Internal Structure of Massive Terrestrial Planets', Icarus 181:545 — arXiv:astro-ph/0511150, https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0511150 (abstract + Table 1 loaded)

findings.claim: Refined interior models with the Vinet EOS and post-perovskite give β = 0.262 for Earth-composition planets (0.244 at 50% H₂O), i.e. g ∝ R^1.82. Verbatim: 'the exponent of the power law becomes smaller: β = 0.262. It is different from 1/3 - the constant density scaling value - due mostly to pressure effects.'
findings.sourceRef: Valencia, Sasselov & O'Connell 2007, 'Detailed Models of super-Earths: How well can we infer bulk properties?', ApJ 665:1413 — arXiv:0704.3454, https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.3454 (§5 Mass-Radius Relationship + Table 1 loaded)

findings.claim: Mantle thickness scales slightly SUPER-linearly with radius: from Valencia 2006 Table 1, mantle thickness D ∝ M^0.286–0.316 while total R ∝ M^0.263–0.272, so d_mantle ∝ R^1.05–1.20. Core radius scales SUB-linearly (R_core ∝ M^0.217–0.258 ⇒ R_core ∝ R^0.83–0.95), so the mantle occupies a growing fraction of a larger planet. This is the derivation behind p_B = +1.10, and it is derived, not assumed.
findings.sourceRef: Valencia, O'Connell & Sasselov 2006, Icarus 181:545 — arXiv:astro-ph/0511150 Table 1 (columns R, D, R_c, ρ_b), https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0511150

findings.claim: Spherical-harmonic DEGREE and physical WAVELENGTH scale differently with R and must never be interchanged. The Jeans relation, verbatim: 'for a given spherical harmonic degree l, the equivalent Cartesian wavelength is λ ≈ 2πR/√(l(l+1)), where R is the mean planetary radius.' Degree is dimensionless (R-independent); wavelength at fixed degree is EXACTLY ∝ R. Degree l=1 → λ = 4.443·R; l=2 → λ = 2.565·R (28,300 km and 16,300 km at Earth).
findings.sourceRef: Wieczorek 2007, 'The gravity and topography of the terrestrial planets', Treatise on Geophysics vol.10 ch.5 — preprint PDF loaded from https://www.whoi.edu/fileserver.do?id=107644&pt=10&p=68153 (§2.1 Spherical harmonics)

findings.claim: Planetary topography spectra are red across Earth, Venus, Mars and the Moon, so spectral power always peaks at the lowest degrees (l=1–2); the peak degree does NOT shift with planet size. Wieczorek notes Venus's spectrum is 'similar to those of the Earth, with the exception that the amplitudes of the degree-1 and -2 topographic terms for Venus are relatively smaller', and a change in slope near degree 100. Practical consequence: the longest topographic wavelength on any terrestrial planet is 2.6–4.4 R, i.e. p = +1.00 exactly.
findings.sourceRef: Wieczorek 2007, Treatise on Geophysics vol.10 ch.5, §3.2.1 Venus / §3.4.3 Moon — https://www.whoi.edu/fileserver.do?id=107644&pt=10&p=68153

findings.claim: There is a UNIVERSAL topographic scale break at ~10–20 km on Earth, Mars, Mercury AND the Moon — bodies spanning 0.27–1.0 R_⊕ — with roughness exponent H ≈ 0.77–0.92 below the break and H = 0.23–0.53 above it. The authors attribute it to lithospheric ELASTIC THICKNESS T_e: below T_e a load is not isostatically compensated and relief persists; above T_e isostasy opposes it. That the break sits at the same absolute km on a 0.27 R_⊕ body and a 1.0 R_⊕ body is direct evidence that the shallow wavelength scale does NOT go as R.
findings.sourceRef: Landais, Schmidt & Lovejoy 2018, 'Multifractal topography of several planetary bodies in the Solar System', arXiv:1805.11249, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.11249 (Table 2 + Discussion)

findings.claim: Venus falsifies any 'break ∝ R' model outright: at 0.95 R_⊕ and 0.90 g its roughness crossover is at 50 km versus Earth's 10 km — 5× larger on a very slightly smaller planet — with the same self-affine exponent α ≈ 0.40 above the break and α ≈ 1.0 below it. Verbatim: 'The self-affine behavior at long scales is achieved on Earth above 10 km and on Venus above 50 km.' The authors explicitly state the mechanism setting the crossover is NOT established.
findings.sourceRef: Crooks, Bar-Yam, Buldyrev & Stanley (dated 1998, posted 2018), 'Comparison of the roughness scaling of the surface topography of Earth and Venus', arXiv:1809.02457, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.02457 — PREPRINT, no journal venue found

findings.claim: Thermal boundary layer (and hence elastic lithosphere) thickness is set by MARGINAL STABILITY, not by mantle depth: δ = [Ra_c·κ·η/(ρ·α·ΔT·g)]^(1/3) ∝ g^(−1/3), independent of layer thickness d. Valencia et al. confirm the sign directly from their interior models, verbatim: 'the thickness of the boundary layer decreases with increasing mass as a consequence of higher Rayleigh numbers for more massive planets.' Combining with the flexural-parameter definition α_f = [4D/(Δρ g)]^(1/4), D = E·T_e³/[12(1−ν²)], gives λ_flex ∝ T_e^(3/4)·g^(−1/4) ∝ g^(−1/2) ∝ R^(−0.85).
findings.sourceRef: Marginal-stability and flexural-parameter forms are STANDARD (Turcotte & Schubert, Geodynamics) and are stated here as standard, not cited to a loaded source. The boundary-layer-thins-with-mass confirmation IS loaded: Valencia, O'Connell & Sasselov 2006, arXiv:astro-ph/0511150, https://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0511150

findings.claim: Earth flexural anchor, computed in this run: with T_e = 30 km (oceanic), E = 100 GPa, ν = 0.25, Δρ = 2300 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², flexural rigidity D = 2.40×10²³ N·m, flexural parameter α_f = 81 km, and flexural wavelength 2π·α_f = 507 km. This is the λ_C,⊕ anchor for range-width / forebulge-spacing features. Note it is a DIFFERENT observable from the 10 km roughness break (which tracks T_e itself, not 2πα_f) — do not conflate the two anchors.
findings.sourceRef: Arithmetic performed in this run from the standard thin-plate flexure formulas; no single paper loaded for this number.

findings.claim: Tectonic plate areas follow a single continuous power law with cumulative exponent 0.25 ± 0.05, expressed in STERADIANS, with the upper cutoff set by the constraint that plate areas must sum to 4π sr. Verbatim abstract: 'the power law with exponent 0.25 +- 0.05 is the most robust and parsimonious model for all plates, including the very largest plates, when taking into account the constraint that the plates areas must sum up to 4 pi steradians.' A distribution that is dimensionless on the sphere with only a 4π cutoff implies plate LINEAR size ∝ R exactly — the empirical backing for p_B ≈ 1.0.
findings.sourceRef: Sornette & Pisarenko 2003, 'Fractal Plate Tectonics', Geophys. Res. Lett. 30(3):1105 — arXiv:cond-mat/0202320 abstract page loaded, https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0202320

findings.claim: Independent re-analysis of the same plate data (52 plates from Bird 2003; 20 from Gurnis et al. 2012) rejects Bird's discrete subpopulations in favour of a continuous 'broken sheet' density function with exponentially distributed plate DIAMETERS (R² = 0.87–0.93), in which size frequencies depend 'only on the total area and number of designated elements'. This too makes plate size a pure function of total surface area (∝ R²), i.e. linear size ∝ R. The paper does not relate plate size to mantle depth or planetary radius directly — that connection is my inference, not theirs.
findings.sourceRef: Wilkinson, McElroy & Dummond 2018, 'Broken Sheets—On the Numbers and Areas of Tectonic Plates', GSA Today 28(6), doi:10.1130/GSATG358A.1 — https://www.geosociety.org/gsa-today/june-2018/broken-sheetson-the-numbers-and-areas-of-tectonic-plates

findings.claim: Plate size on Earth is physically controlled by SUBDUCTION GEOMETRY — slab spacing sets the layout of large plates, and trench-bending stresses fragment plates into small ones. If that mechanism generalises, large plates track the convective wavelength (∝ d_mantle ∝ R^1.1) while small fragments track lithospheric thickness (∝ g^−1/3 ∝ R^−0.57), which would naturally produce Bird's two apparent subpopulations diverging with planet size. THE DIVERGING-SUBPOPULATION INFERENCE IS MINE, NOT THE PAPER'S, and is untested.
findings.sourceRef: Mallard, Coltice, Seton, Müller & Tackley 2016, Nature 535:140–143, doi:10.1038/nature17992 — NOT LOADED this run (search-result summary only). Kept out of the load-bearing argument.

findings.claim: The simple→complex crater transition goes as ~1/g and the codebase's K_DT = 3.1 is CORRECT. Verbatim: 'Since the transition from simple to complex structures is a function of surface gravity (g), with a roughly 1/g dependence, it occurs at different diameters on different planetary bodies... On the Moon, the simple-to-complex transition occurs at approximately 20 km' (average ~19 km). Check: 19–20 km × g_Moon 0.165 = K = 3.1–3.3. The repo's 3.1 km·g_⊕ lands squarely on the lunar anchor. No change needed.
findings.sourceRef: Silber, Osinski, Johnson & Grieve 2017, 'Effect of impact velocity and acoustic fluidization on the simple-to-complex transition of lunar craters', JGR-Planets, doi:10.1002/2016JE005236 — arXiv:1704.04247, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.04247 (Introduction)

findings.claim: Second, independent confirmation of D_t ∝ 1/g with the underlying Pike thresholds, verbatim: 'The data for lunar craters by Pike 1977 gives a transition to complex shapes beginning at D*=10.6 km rim diameter. The transition in rim heights begins at a larger size, D*rh=22.8 km diameter. The onset of flat floors is gradual, but is fully developed at D*fl=20 km diameter. On the earth, those transition diameters are reduced by the inverse of the gravity levels (Pike, 1977).' So K_DT is threshold-definition-dependent: ONSET K≈1.75, FLAT-FLOOR K≈3.30, RIM-HEIGHT K≈3.76. The repo's 3.1 sits at the flat-floor/fully-complex end — the conservative choice, and defensible.
findings.sourceRef: Holsapple 2022, 'IMPACTS! A program to calculate the effects of a hypervelocity impact into a Solar System body', arXiv:2203.07476, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.07476 (§3.6 Complex Craters)

findings.claim: AUDIT DEFECT: the codebase's K_GS = 0.17 (D ∝ g^−0.17) is the DRY-SAND value, not the rocky value. The gravity-regime diameter exponent is μ/(2+μ). Verbatim from Holsapple: 'for relatively dissipative materials such as "dry" soils and sands the exponent µ is about 0.4, and for wet and rocky targets it is about 0.55.' His Table 1 lists Hard Rocks μ=0.55, Dry Sand μ=0.4, Lunar Regolith μ=0.4, Cold Ice μ=0.55. μ=0.4 → 0.167 (matches 0.17); μ=0.55 → 0.216. A silicate-crust or icy-crust world should use 0.22; the repo's existing `rockyCrust` discriminator is the natural switch.
findings.sourceRef: Holsapple 2022, arXiv:2203.07476 §3.1–3.2 and Table 1, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.07476

findings.claim: D_t ∝ 1/g has a known, sign-determined offset that will matter on super-Earths: Mercury's observed complex-crater onset is 1.5–2× larger than the pure-gravity prediction, attributed to its high median impact velocity (42.5 km/s). Since v_impact² = v_∞² + v_esc² and v_esc ∝ √(gR) ∝ R^1.35, super-Earths impact far harder than Earth, so real super-Earth D_t should sit ABOVE 3.1/g — plausibly by the same 1.5–2× factor. Verbatim: 'On Mercury, the onset of complex structures (e.g., flat floor, terracing) occurs at a factor of 1.5-2 larger than expected diameters... even when gravity is taken into consideration'.
findings.sourceRef: Silber, Osinski, Johnson & Grieve 2017, JGR-Planets doi:10.1002/2016JE005236 — arXiv:1704.04247 (Discussion), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.04247

findings.claim: Aeolian dune wavelength contains NO gravity and NO planet-radius term. Verbatim: 'we obtain a consistent scaling law λ ≃ 53·L_drag that covers almost five decades', with L_drag = (ρ_s/ρ_f)·d, ρ_s/ρ_f the grain-to-fluid density ratio and d the grain diameter. Tested in water, in air, in fresh snow, in a high-pressure CO₂ wind tunnel reproducing Venus conditions, and against martian dunes. Computed anchors from the law: Earth (2650/1.2, 180 µm) → λ = 21 m; Mars (2900/0.02, 100 µm) → λ = 0.77 km, matching the paper's remark that martian dunes are 'of the order of a kilometre'.
findings.sourceRef: Claudin & Andreotti 2006, 'A scaling law for aeolian dunes on Mars, Venus, Earth, and for subaqueous ripples', EPSL 252:30–44 — arXiv:cond-mat/0603656, https://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0603656

findings.claim: Fluvial ridge-and-valley wavelength contains NO gravity and NO planet-radius term either. The characteristic length is L_c = (D/K)^(1/(2m+1)) from setting a Péclet-like number Pe = K·L^(2m+1)/D equal to 1 (D = soil-creep diffusivity, K = stream-incision coefficient, m = drainage-area exponent), and the emergent valley spacing satisfies 6.4·L_c ≤ λ ≤ 12.7·L_c.
